results.key_finding: High-efficacy DMTs (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine) produce substantially lower relapse rates and MRI activity compared to platform agents in highly active RRMS. Evidence supports early initiation of high-efficacy therapy in patients with rapidly accruing disability or high lesion burden to maximise NEDA-3 (no evidence of disease activity: no relapses, no disability progression, no new MRI lesions).
results.source: Reich DS, Lucchinetti CF, Calabresi PA. Multiple Sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2018;378:169-180
results.title: High-efficacy therapies in multiple sclerosis: evidence for early aggressive treatment

results.key_finding: Anti-JCV antibody index above 1.5 in previously natalizumab-naive patients is associated with a substantially elevated PML risk (estimated 1:200 to 1:100 at 24 months) compared to JCV-negative patients (estimated risk <1:10,000). An index >1.5 significantly limits natalizumab use; JCV-negative patients can be started on natalizumab with scheduled re-testing every 6 months.
results.title: JC virus antibody status and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk with natalizumab

results.key_finding: Highly active RRMS is defined by: (a) ≥2 disabling relapses in one year on platform therapy, or (b) ≥1 relapse plus ≥1 gadolinium-enhancing or ≥9 T2 lesions untreated. For such patients high-efficacy DMTs are preferred. Pre-treatment screening includes hepatitis B/C, HIV, JCV serology, CBC, LFTs, and varicella zoster IgG status.
results.source: Montalban X et al. Multiple Sclerosis Journal 2018
results.title: ECTRIMS/EAN 2018 guideline: pharmacological treatment of multiple sclerosis

output.summary: In highly active RRMS (multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions, high T2 burden, recurrent relapses), high-efficacy DMTs (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine) are preferred over platform agents to achieve NEDA-3. Anti-JCV antibody index is the principal risk-stratification tool for natalizumab PML risk: index >1.5 substantially elevates PML risk and generally precludes natalizumab initiation. Pre-DMT screening (hepatitis B/C, HIV, JCV, VZV, CBC, LFTs) is mandatory before initiating any high-efficacy agent.

alternatives: Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20, high efficacy, IV every 6 months) — preferred when JCV index precludes natalizumab
Ofatumumab (anti-CD20, high efficacy, subcutaneous) — alternative to ocrelizumab
Cladribine (oral, annual short courses) — effective option; contraception required
Alemtuzumab — highest efficacy; significant monitoring burden (autoimmune adverse effects)
contraindications: Natalizumab: Contraindicated in patients with prior or current progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). High anti-JCV antibody index (>1.5) substantially increases estimated PML risk (estimated 1:200 to 1:100 over 24 months in anti-JCV-positive, natalizumab-naive patients with index >1.5); use requires formal benefit-risk discussion and typically is avoided when alternative high-efficacy options exist.

Live-attenuated vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella-zoster live, yellow fever, oral typhoid): Contraindicated during and for at least 1 month after B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab); generally contraindicated during cladribine treatment and for 12 months after. Live vaccines should ideally be administered and documented as current before any of these agents are started.
Cladribine: Avoid in pregnancy and ensure effective contraception throughout treatment and for 6 months after the last dose; teratogenic in animal models.

interactions: Levonorgestrel-ethinyl estradiol (oral contraceptive): No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction with natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, or cladribine
Ibuprofen (as-needed NSAID): No significant interaction with any listed high-efficacy DMT class

warnings: Natalizumab: Mandatory JCV antibody status assessment before initiation and every 6 months during therapy; TOUCH program enrollment required in the United States
Ocrelizumab: Screen for hepatitis B reactivation risk (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before initiation; hold for active serious infection; monitor immunoglobulin levels with prolonged use

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT initiate a low-efficacy platform DMT (interferon-β, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide) as the primary treatment for this highly active presentation — rapidly accruing disability and high lesion burden in a young patient favour early high-efficacy therapy over an escalation approach

Do NOT start natalizumab given the high anti-JCV antibody index (2.84); the estimated PML risk at this index level (1:100 to 1:200 over 24 months) is generally considered to outweigh the benefit when equivalent high-efficacy alternatives are available
Do NOT omit anti-JCV antibody testing before any MS DMT decision — it is a mandatory part of the pre-treatment safety screen and directly governs natalizumab eligibility
Do NOT administer live-attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella-zoster live, yellow fever, oral typhoid) after initiating ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, or cladribine
Do NOT use chronic oral corticosteroids for MS maintenance — they are ineffective for disease modification and cause long-term harm
Do NOT order CT of the brain as the primary or sole imaging modality — MRI with gadolinium is required to characterise lesion burden and enhancement
required_recommendations: Recognise that this presentation represents HIGHLY ACTIVE RRMS: multiple (≥4) gadolinium-enhancing lesions, high T2 lesion burden (≥14 lesions), relapsing course with incomplete recovery over ≥18 months — this phenotype mandates early high-efficacy DMT rather than platform therapy

Obtain anti-JCV antibody (STRATIFY index) as part of pre-DMT screening: a high index (here 2.84, far above the 1.5 threshold) substantially elevates PML risk with natalizumab and should direct DMT selection away from natalizumab toward alternatives (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine)

Establish the 2024 revised McDonald DIS and DIT criteria formally: multiple enhancing and non-enhancing lesions across periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions amply fulfil DIS; simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions establish DIT on this scan alone
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before DMT initiation — negative here but required to close the differential given spinal cord and optic nerve involvement
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g IV daily for 3–5 days); consider plasma exchange if steroid-refractory within 7 days

Complete pre-DMT infectious panel (hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV IgG) before initiating any high-efficacy agent; live vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever) must be administered before starting B-cell-depleting therapy
Refer to or consult an MS subspecialist for DMT selection, given the high JCV index and complex risk-benefit calculation between high-efficacy options

Counsel the patient on oral contraception and teratogenicity: teriflunomide and cladribine require strict contraception; ocrelizumab has limited human pregnancy data — coordinate with obstetric/gynaecology if conception is planned

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific for MS and does not contribute to dissemination in space or time; no seizure or encephalopathy presentation.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for demyelinating plaques; ordering CT adds radiation without diagnostic yield and would delay MRI-based workup.
No cardiac indication in this MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential or DMT decision.
Holter monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod (bradyarrhythmia monitoring) — not part of MS diagnosis or high-efficacy DMT (natalizumab/ocrelizumab/cladribine) pre-treatment workup.
FDG-PET has no role in MS diagnosis or high-efficacy DMT selection; it does not differentiate demyelination from its mimics and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Highly active RRMS is defined radiographically by multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions and/or ≥9 T2 lesions at onset, plus a relapsing clinical course — this patient meets both criteria and warrants early high-efficacy DMT

The anti-JCV antibody index (2.84) is a critical management pivot: while natalizumab is the prototypical high-efficacy option, an index >1.5 substantially increases estimated PML risk and should redirect DMT selection to ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, or cladribine

NEDA-3 (no evidence of disease activity: zero relapses, zero confirmed disability progression, zero new or enlarging MRI lesions) is the treatment target in highly active RRMS; high-efficacy DMTs have superior NEDA-3 rates versus platform agents

The heavy lesion burden with multiple enhancing lesions may raise concern for ADEM or a vasculitic/tumefactive process; the relapsing course over >18 months, typical Dawson-finger morphology, OCB positivity, and negative DWI/ESR/CRP distinguish highly active RRMS from these mimics

CSF-restricted OCBs (7 bands, IgG index 0.94) strongly support intrathecal inflammatory demyelination and fulfil the 2024 revised McDonald DIT criterion when used alongside DIS evidence; the markedly elevated IgG synthesis rate reflects the high inflammatory load

Short-segment (<2 vertebral body) peripheral/dorsolateral cord lesions at C3-C4, C6, and T4-T5 are consistent with MS and distinguish this from NMOSD (which produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 24-year-old right-handed woman of Hispanic descent who presented to the neurology inpatient service with a 3-week history of worsening right leg weakness, sensory disturbance in the right side, and new urinary urgency. She reports that her symptoms began approximately 21 days ago when she noticed heaviness and stiffness in her right leg that has progressively worsened to the point of affecting her gait and causing her to nearly fall twice. Over the past week she has developed mild bilateral lower extremity stiffness. She endorses a tight, band-like burning sensation around her mid-abdomen at the T8 level, intermittent and worsened by exertion. She also has urinary urgency with rare urge incontinence, which she finds socially distressing. She notes that hot showers transiently worsen both the leg weakness and a persistent hazy quality to her right-eye vision — the latter she attributes to a prior episode of 'optic nerve inflammation' 18 months ago from which she never fully recovered. On detailed questioning she recalls a second distinct episode approximately 11 months ago, during which she experienced left leg weakness and an unsteady gait lasting about 3 weeks; this episode was evaluated at urgent care and attributed to 'stress-related functional overlay'; no MRI was performed at that time and the symptoms partially resolved but did not fully remit. She reports persistent fatigue that she describes as a 'heaviness' distinct from her prior normal tiredness. She denies new visual loss, diplopia, dysphagia, arm weakness, cognitive changes, fever, weight loss, oral ulcers, joint pain, or skin rash. She has a family history notable for her mother having multiple sclerosis. She has not had any vaccinations in the past year. She is sexually active and uses oral contraception. She has no prior MS diagnosis and has never been on any disease-modifying therapy.
